📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, alzheimer's disease may begin leaving detectable clues in the brain as much as a decade before memory problems appear.
  • The discovery could eventually help doctors recognize Alzheimer's years before symptoms develop, potentially allowing treatment to begin when it has the greatest chance of protecting the brain.
  • Sources indicate that by examining hundreds of brain scans, the scientists found that the entorhinal cortex and amygdala, two regions involved in memory and emotion, begin losing tissue earlier than the hippocampus.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, alzheimer's disease may begin leaving detectable clues in the brain as much as a decade before memory problems appear. Researchers at Johns Hopkins University have identified two brain regions that show signs of deterioration earlier than the hippocampus, the area commonly examined for evidence of the disease.

The discovery could eventually help doctors recognize Alzheimer's years before symptoms develop, potentially allowing treatment to begin when it has the greatest chance of protecting the brain.

Sources indicate that by examining hundreds of brain scans, the scientists found that the entorhinal cortex and amygdala, two regions involved in memory and emotion, begin losing tissue earlier than the hippocampus. These changes may offer important fresh clues about how Alzheimer's develops and how it could be detected before significant cognitive decline occurs.

"We have found that there are early changes in the brain manifesting the clinical biomarkers of atrophy as much as a decade before there are clinical symptoms," said biomedical engineer and senior author Michael Miller. "It's at least a 5-to-10-year play where your brain is changing. Imagine if we could start to treat the neurodegenerative changes at the 2, 3 or 4-year point rather than after 15 years when the changes are manifesting in memory symptoms. That's the great promise here for your loved ones who are at risk.".

The findings were recently published in NeuroImage Reports and are being presented at Neuroscience 2026, the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience.

Detecting Alzheimer's Before Memory Loss Begins.

Alzheimer's is the most common cause of dementia worldwide, but the disease does not begin when someone first experiences forgetfulness or confusion. Changes associated with Alzheimer's can accumulate in the brain for decades before noticeable symptoms emerge.

Recent findings suggest that scientists believe this long period of silent progression may provide a crucial opportunity for treatment. Interventions that begin before extensive damage occurs could potentially do more to preserve memory and other cognitive abilities. However, taking advantage of that opportunity requires reliable ways to identify the disease in its earliest stages.

It has been revealed that one promising approach involves biomarkers, measurable biological changes that can indicate the presence or progression of a disease. In Alzheimer's research, these markers could help reveal who is developing the condition before symptoms become apparent.

"Our goal is to be able to treat individuals before the symptoms of Alzheimer's disease develop so that they may delayed or even stopped," noted Marilyn Albert, co-author and director of the Johns Hopkins Alzheimer's Disease Research Center.

Two Brain Regions Reveal Earlier Warning Signs.

To investigate where the earliest detectable changes occur, the researchers examined hundreds of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and positron emission tomography (PET) scans collected through two independent research projects: the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative and the Biomarkers of Cognitive Decline Among Normal Individuals study.

The scans followed people at different stages of Alzheimer's disease over time, including individuals without symptoms, those experiencing cognitive impairment, and patients who ultimately died from the disease.

In both groups, the researchers observed a consistent pattern. The entorhinal cortex and amygdala, which are located near the hippocampus, showed greater relative tissue loss during the early stages of Alzheimer's than the hippocampus itself.

This distinction matters because the hippocampus plays a central role in memory and has traditionally been a major focus when doctors look for Alzheimer's-related brain damage.

The two newly highlighted regions perform important functions of their own. The entorhinal cortex helps retrieve previously stored memories, while the amygdala contributes to emotional memory, including how emotional experiences are processed and remembered.

Their earlier shrinkage suggests that examining these structures together could reveal signs of Alzheimer's that might be less apparent when attention is focused primarily on the hippocampus.

Brain Shrinkage Linked to Alzheimer's Tau Protein.

The researchers also found an important connection between the loss of brain tissue and tau, a protein closely associated with Alzheimer's disease.

Under normal conditions, tau helps maintain the internal structure of nerve cells. In Alzheimer's, however, tau can accumulate abnormally and form tangles that interfere with healthy brain function.

Using PET imaging and digital pathology, the scientists found that areas of gray matter shrinkage overlapped with regions showing tau-related changes. Gray matter contains large numbers of nerve cell bodies and is essential for processing information throughout the brain.

This relationship strengthens the possibility that changes in the entorhinal cortex and amygdala could serve as useful indicators of early Alzheimer's disease.

The team believes that measuring tissue loss in both regions, rather than relying primarily on changes in the hippocampus, could eventually improve predictions of who is likely to develop cognitive decline.

According to recent reports, as brain imaging becomes more accessible and less expensive, this approach could also become increasingly practical. For people with a family history of Alzheimer's or other risk factors, researchers envision a future in which doctors might examine these regions as early as a person's 30s or 40s.

"As biomarkers and treatments become increasingly available, knowing who is going to have cognitive decline is going to be really important," noted co-author Meaghan Morris, a neuropathologist who studies Alzheimer's and other dementias. "This could really play into better risk stratification for identifying who is going to have cognitive decline in the near future -- and treating people earlier and earlier to hopefully slow the course of the disease.".

A Potential Newly introduced Path Toward Earlier Alzheimer's Treatment.

According to recent reports, although the findings are promising, more research is necessary before doctors can use these brain changes as a reliable diagnostic tool. The study identifies potential early biomarkers, but it does not yet establish a clinical test capable of predicting Alzheimer's years in advance.

In a recent development, the next step is to investigate what happens within these regions at a much smaller scale. The researchers want to understand the molecular changes surrounding abnormal tau accumulation and how those changes contribute to the progressive loss of brain tissue.

Identifying the biological processes involved could eventually reveal newly introduced targets for therapies designed to interrupt Alzheimer's before extensive damage occurs.

"Our future work is to better show the molecular neighborhoods associated with these Tau protein changes as localized by these clinical biomarkers of atrophy," Miller stated. "Once we know more about the molecular neighborhoods, we can develop therapies.".

Materials provided by Johns Hopkins University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

CMS issues Medicare Advantage proposals aimed at boosting competition" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Trump administration has proposed a slew of changes to Medicare Advantage and Part D designed to "revitalize care" in these markets.

For one, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services noted late Friday that it will upgrade application and network adequacy requirements to make it easier for latest entrants. The agency proposed to require organizations to demonstrate network adequacy during their first year in operation, rather than during the application process.

This shift would eliminate a significant barrier for new entrants, driving greater competition in the market.

CMS has also proposed combining three specialty areas in behavioral health—clinical psychology, clinical social work and outpatient behavioral health—into one specialty group for the purposes of network adequacy. The changes will give looks greater flexibility in building out behavioral health networks.

CMS will also make adjustments that seek to boost competition for special needs plans.

It has been revealed that in addition, the agency mentioned it will make adjustments to the star ratings program, focusing its ratings on 15 measures. The proposed measure set would emphasize "clinical outcomes and patient experience while retaining select process measures in high-priority areas where performance remains low.".

CMS is also aiming to revision the calculation methodology that will "raise the bar for achieving high ratings," and thus quality bonus payments.

In a recent development, "People with Medicare should be able to choose coverage based on what matters most to them—quality, affordability and access," remarked CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., in the announcement. "These proposals are about creating a Medicare Advantage marketplace that rewards better care and better value while empowering beneficiaries with the options and knowledge they need to make informed decisions about their health.".

The proposed rule also includes provisions that align with Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy's Make America Healthy Again agenda by setting a "healthy food" standard that MA plans should follow for supplemental benefits.

The goal, CMS said, is to ensure that Medicare dollars are spent on food benefits that align with MAHA.

"Medicare food benefits should pay for nutritious food that helps people improve their health and manage chronic disease," Kennedy stated in the announcement. "This proposal would require those benefits to meet the Dietary Guidelines for Americans while preserving access to foods and nutritional products that providers recommend for patients’ specific medical needs.".

"Under President Trump, we are putting prevention at the center of health care and demanding more from every Medicare dollar," Kennedy said.

Photon pharmacy marketplace integrated with ChatGPT for clinicians" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Photon, a prescription infrastructure company, is now available as a plugin for ChatGPT to streamline prescribing for clinicians within a tool they already use.

According to recent reports, the option is available to eligible U.S. licensed clinicians using ChatGPT for Clinicians (free for verified clinicians) or ChatGPT for Healthcare. Just as clinicians must accept OpenAI’s BAA before sharing protected patient information, they must accept Photon’s BAA to maintain HIPAA compliance when using Photon in ChatGPT. Controlled substances are not supported. The feature is free for clinicians through Dec. 31, 2026.

It has been revealed that the patient experience remains the same through Photon. What is new is where the clinician can write a prescription. Clinicians with a Photon account can draft, review and send prescriptions without leaving ChatGPT. They just need to add the Photon plugin into ChatGPT, and then they can draft prescriptions. A patient will get a text to Photon’s prescription marketplace outside of ChatGPT. Patients can compare prices and request to change a pharmacy as needed.

According to recent reports, “AI is moving from note-taking and reference into treatment workflows. Clinicians are already using ChatGPT to understand treatment options. Once they’ve decided what to prescribe, they should be able to act on that decision in the same conversation,” Otto Sipe, co-founder and CEO, wrote to Fierce Healthcare in an emailed comment. “Photon provides the infrastructure behind that step.”.

In the newly introduced interface, clinicians begin a prompt with the name of the patient and medication. Photon uses authorized patient information and treatment context shared with ChatGPT to help prepare a prescription for a clinician’s review. They can also add new patient details during the process. Once saved in Photon, that patient can be found by name for future prescriptions.

It has been revealed that from there, clinicians review the prescribing details, including the dosing, instructions and quantity. Clinicians can ask about dosing options in the chat. Patient records are saved in Photon, and draft prescriptions are checked against the patient’s recorded allergies and medications. Finally, clinicians review and authorize the prescription to be sent, remaining responsible for the treatment. Clinicians can check a prescription’s status in ChatGPT.

  • While we sleep, the brain carries out an essential maintenance process that helps wash away accumulated waste.
  • According to recent reports, researchers discovered that waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which help carry waste out of the brain, are significantly weaker in older adults.
  • In a recent development, the findings raise key questions about whether weakened brain cleansing could contribute to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While we sleep, the brain carries out an essential maintenance process that helps wash away accumulated waste. But newly introduced research from MIT suggests that this natural cleaning system becomes less effective as we grow older, revealing another way aging can change the brain beyond simply disrupting sleep.

According to recent reports, researchers discovered that waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which help carry waste out of the brain, are significantly weaker in older adults. The decline appears to be connected to changes in the slow electrical waves that occur during deep sleep, as well as changes in how blood moves through the brain. Importantly, the reduced fluid movement cannot be explained simply by older people spending less time asleep.

In a recent development, the findings raise key questions about whether weakened brain cleansing could contribute to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. The team now hopes to determine whether changes in these fluid waves could eventually help identify people at greater risk of cognitive decline.

Industry observers note that "We know that people age really differently. Some people age very successfully with great cognitive outcomes, and other people develop cognitive decline. If we can figure out who has great trajectories of aging and what are the factors that are associated with that, we might be able to use that to predict future outcomes," notes Laura Lewis, the Athinoula A. Martinos Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, a member of MIT's Institute for Medical Engineering and Science and the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and an associate member of the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory.

Lewis and her colleagues also want to investigate whether treatments or other interventions could strengthen this waste-clearing process in older adults.

The study was published in Nature Aging, with Lewis serving as senior author. Its lead authors are Sydney Bailes, a postdoctoral researcher in MIT's Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems, and Stephanie Williams, a former MIT visiting student who received her PhD from Boston University in 2026.

How Deep Sleep Helps the Brain Clear Waste.

It has been revealed that deep sleep does much more than leave us feeling refreshed. During its deepest stages, known as non-REM sleep, the brain produces powerful, slow electrical waves that support physical recovery, strengthen memories, and help regulate other essential functions.

In 2019, Lewis and her colleagues discovered that these slow brain waves also help generate rhythmic movements of cerebrospinal fluid. The fluid moves through spaces around the brain and plays an notable role in carrying away waste products.

That earlier discovery led to a newly introduced question. Because slow brain waves typically weaken with age, could the fluid movements responsible for clearing waste also become less effective?

Industry observers note that previous research had produced conflicting results. Some studies suggested that cerebrospinal fluid movement declined with age, while others reported increases. However, those investigations had not directly monitored the fluid during sleep, when the brain's natural cleaning activity is especially important.

In a recent development, to investigate, the MIT team recruited two groups of volunteers. Younger participants were between 18 and 39 years old, while the older group ranged from 60 to 84.

Each volunteer completed a testing session lasting approximately two hours. The sessions began late at night, increasing the likelihood that participants would become sleepy during the measurements.

The researchers combined several techniques to observe what was happening inside the brain. Functional magnetic resonance imaging, or fMRI, allowed them to track changes in cerebral blood flow. A specialized MRI method developed by Lewis measured cerebrospinal fluid movement, while electroencephalography, or EEG, recorded the brain's electrical activity.

Many participants fell asleep inside the scanner, providing an opportunity to compare their brain activity and fluid movements during wakefulness and sleep.

It has been revealed that the results revealed a striking age difference. As younger adults entered non-REM sleep, their slow brain waves grew stronger and were accompanied by larger waves of cerebrospinal fluid. In older adults, however, the average fluid waves were substantially smaller.

The findings revealed that aging was associated with a weakening of the fluid movements that normally accompany deep sleep.

Why the Aging Brain's Cleaning Waves Weaken.

The researchers next investigated what might be causing this decline. In a separate set of experiments conducted while participants were fully awake, they examined how the brain's blood vessels responded to different demands.

One possible explanation involved neurovascular coupling, the process that connects brain activity with blood flow.

Sources indicate that when a particular region of the brain becomes more active, its cells require additional oxygen and nutrients. Nearby blood vessels normally widen to deliver more blood, ensuring that the active cells receive the resources they need.

According to recent reports, to measure this response, the researchers showed volunteers a flickering checkerboard pattern while monitoring blood flow with fMRI. The rapidly changing visual pattern stimulates activity in regions involved in processing vision, which should trigger an increase in local blood supply.

In many older participants, the brain's electrical activity increased as expected, but the corresponding rise in blood flow was much smaller. This suggested that aging had weakened the ability of blood vessels to respond to the brain's changing oxygen requirements.

The team then performed a second experiment to examine the brain's broader vascular responsiveness.

Sources indicate that participants were instructed to hold their breath while researchers monitored changes in cerebral blood flow. Holding one's breath causes carbon dioxide to accumulate in the bloodstream, which normally prompts blood vessels in the brain to widen and increase blood flow.

Industry observers note that once again, the older group indicated a weaker response. On average, their cerebral blood flow increased less than it did in younger volunteers.

Together, these experiments indicated that changes in the brain's vascular system could help explain why its waste-clearing fluid waves diminish with age.

Industry observers note that using a statistical model, the scientists found that weakened neurovascular coupling and reduced blood flow responses accounted for much of the decline in cerebrospinal fluid movement. However, the two mechanisms did not explain the entire difference, suggesting that additional biological changes associated with aging are also involved.

It has been revealed that "Aging is so complex, and so many different things change, that it's really hard to disentangle the individual factors," Bailes says. "We try to account for some of the mechanisms, but there definitely are a lot of other factors related to vascular health and lifestyle. If you were able to measure all of them, you might be able to break it apart into different explanations for why an individual's CSF flow might be more or less impaired.".

Could Weaker Brain Cleansing Increase Dementia Risk?

The discovery may have crucial implications for understanding neurological diseases associated with aging.

Recent findings suggest that earlier studies have linked disrupted sleep to a greater risk of Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. Because cerebrospinal fluid helps remove waste from the brain, researchers are particularly interested in whether age-related changes in its movement might contribute to neurodegeneration.

Sources indicate that none of the volunteers in the MIT study had been diagnosed with a neurodegenerative disorder. However, brain scans revealed that some older participants showed signs of gray matter atrophy, meaning a loss of brain tissue in regions containing large numbers of nerve cells.

Those changes were associated with greater reductions in cerebrospinal fluid movement.

Sources indicate that the relationship does not establish that weakened fluid flow causes brain tissue loss or dementia. Nevertheless, it provides a reason to investigate whether these changes might serve as early warning signs of neurological decline.

The researchers hope to follow some of the participants over time to determine whether reduced cerebrospinal fluid movement is associated with a greater likelihood of developing a neurodegenerative condition.

Can the Brain's Nighttime Cleaning System Be Restored?

Beyond understanding why brain cleansing declines, the MIT team is exploring whether it might be possible to improve the process.

One promising possibility involves sound stimulation during sleep.

Recent findings suggest that in a separate recent study, Lewis' laboratory found that brief bursts of "pink noise" could increase cerebrospinal fluid movement in younger adults. Pink noise is a type of sound that contains a broad range of frequencies, with greater emphasis on lower frequencies than white noise.

Although the approach has shown potential in younger people, researchers have not yet tested whether it can produce similar effects in older adults.

Another intriguing finding could provide clues about how to preserve the brain's natural cleaning abilities.

Recent findings suggest that while older participants generally had weaker cerebrospinal fluid waves than younger adults, the decline was not universal. Some older volunteers retained fluid movements that were comparable to those measured in healthy younger people.

This raises the possibility that certain biological or lifestyle factors may help protect the brain's waste-removal system against aging.

"It's really intriguing that for some of these older adults, their CSF fell right in the range of the healthy young adults," Lewis says. "We are really interested in what's different in those people and how that might be related to future health outcomes.".

Understanding why some older brains maintain these youthful fluid movements could ultimately help researchers identify ways to support healthier brain aging and investigate whether preserving the brain's nighttime cleaning system can reduce the risk of cognitive decline.

The research received funding from the National Institutes of Health, the Simons Collaboration on Plasticity in the Aging Brain, a McKnight Scholar Award, a Pew Biomedical Scholar Award, an MIT EECS Transformative Research Award, the Picower Institute Neurological Disorder Discovery Research Fund, a Sloan Fellowship, and the Department of Defense National Defense Science and Engineering Graduate Fellowship Program.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • However, the companies have very different prospects going forward as they try to come to terms with the diverging fortunes of the artificial intelligence server and personal computer markets they serve.
  • Dell reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of $9.45 per share on revenue of $54.94 billion, a stunning result that blew past Wall Street’s expectations of just $6.59 per share in earnings and $49.32 billion in sales.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:48 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Updated with Wednesday stock prices:.

Sources indicate that dell Technologies Inc. and HP Inc. delivered strong earnings and revenue beats as they posted their latest financial results today.

However, the companies have very different prospects going forward as they try to come to terms with the diverging fortunes of the artificial intelligence server and personal computer markets they serve.

Dell reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of $9.45 per share on revenue of $54.94 billion, a stunning result that blew past Wall Street’s expectations of just $6.59 per share in earnings and $49.32 billion in sales.

Recent findings suggest that the company’s revenue more than doubled from a year earlier thanks to the sky-high demand for the AI servers and related data center infrastructure equipment it sells. Dell’s Infrastructure Solutions Group delivered sales of $41.97 billion during the quarter, far in excess of the Street’s target of $35.27 billion. Of that, around $22 billion came from direct AI-optimized server sales, the company said. That segment was up 291% annually.

“We are now a different company, with the Infrastructure Solutions Group driving the vast majority of our profit and growth,” remarked Dell Vice Chairman and Chief Operating Officer Jeff Clarke (pictured). He added that Dell now has more than 7,500 customers buying its AI servers.

Sources indicate that the Street liked what it saw, with Dell’s stock rising more than 3% after hours, putting the brakes on an 11% decline earlier, during the regular trading session. Revision: However, on another down day for tech stocks Wednesday, Dell’s shares were falling almost 8% before the market cut some of those losses and Dell was falling only a fraction of a point.

Dell’s performance in the quarter sets a new precedent for infrastructure systems companies, mentioned longtime technology industry analyst Dave Vellante, chief analyst at theCUBE Research, SiliconANGLE Media’s sister market research firm.

In a recent development, “Dell has transformed from a PC firm into a dominant enterprise infrastructure provider and industry bellwether,” he said. “What’s most astounding to me is that I’ve always considered AWS to be Dell’s most formidable competitor. Dell is now significantly larger than AWS on a trailing 12-month revenue basis and is growing at a rate that’s more than double that of AWS, Azure and on a par with Google Cloud.”.

According to recent reports, dell is raising its forecast for AI servers in the coming fiscal years, and now sees sales rising to a staggering $78 billion, ahead of the Street’s target of $74 billion. At present, the company has an even bigger order backlog of $132.3 billion for AI servers. “Every order is verified for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance and access to land and power,” Clarke told analysts in response to a question about the reliability of that backlog.

Vellante stated Dell’s operating leverage is just as impressive, with its operating income, net profit and earnings per share all growing at rates over two-times its revenue growth.

“Its massive backlog and strong product execution allow it to be selective,” the analyst said. “Thus the quality of its revenue and its backlog is very high, and the tech giant is well-positioned for the next several quarters. Current market signals point to a structural change in tech where vendors that are in a position to help customers transform and drive newly introduced levels of productivity are poised to win over the long term. We increasingly see Dell as one of those leaders.”.

In a recent development, besides servers, Dell still has a big business in the PC market. Its Client Services Group was once the firm’s biggest segment, but its revenue is now dwarfed by AI server sales. During the quarter, it generated revenue of $12.89 billion, below the Street’s forecast of $14.33 billion.

According to recent reports, the reason for that miss is that the global PC market is presently enduring a sharp decline. Last month, Gartner Inc. reported a stunning 22% drop in global PC shipments in the third quarter, citing the increased costs of components such as memory chips, which have led to higher prices and compelled many people to hold onto their older laptops for longer.

According to recent reports, the miserable state of PC sales makes HP’s latest quarterly results seem even more impressive than they were. However, the firm’s cautious outlook suggests that its incoming Chief Executive Emma Walmsley (pictured, right) will have her work cut out when she assumes the role full time on Jan. 4, when she’s slated to take over from interim CEO Bruce Broussard.

In a recent development, HP reported fourth-quarter adjusted earnings of 83 cents per share, surpassing the analyst consensus estimate that called for a profit of just 75 cents per share. Revenue for the period came to $16 billion, up 9% and above the Street’s target of $15.4 billion.

HP’s stock briefly surged more than 17% after-hours, before promptly surrendering all of those gains in under an hour. It was down just under a percentage point at the time of writing. Upgrade: On Wednesday, investors appeared to change their minds again, as the stock was rising more than 12%.

In a recent development, investors had low expectations of HP given the shoddy state of the PC market. The manufacturer has been trying to mitigate the situation somewhat by raising its prices, but it couldn’t stop its profit margins from declining in the quarter.

According to recent reports, the market was eagerly anticipating HP’s guidance to try and get a lid on whether or not the PC market has any prospect of recovery in the near future, but the tech giant disappointed by refusing to provide any. All it would say is that it forecasts free cash flow in the current quarter to be $3 billion, plus or minus $100 million. Analysts are targeting free cash flow of $3.3 billion.

It has been revealed that HP hasn’t been helped by the fact that it has been without a CEO since PayPal Holdings Inc. surprisingly swooped in to poach its former leader Enrique Lores in February. Broussard has held the fort for close to nine months now, but the manufacturer did at least finally name a successor in Walmsley, who will begin her tenure next year. She formerly led the pharmaceutical giant GSK Plc.

Walmsley has a tough act to follow, however, for Broussard has done rather well in his efforts to cope with the PC market downturn and the higher component costs. Although the stock was up and down today, it’s still up 25% in the year to date.
