The Virginia Department of Health confirmed on Nov. 20 its first measles-associated death since 1978.

According to recent reports, the individual was a child younger than four years of age who had tested positive for measles, though the state has refrained from providing more information about the case for privacy reasons. The state has reported 220 cases in total this year, as of a Nov. 19 dashboard upgrade, with most occurring in its central region and at least 179 of which were confirmed to be unvaccinated.

In a recent development, it is the fourth state this year to have reported a measles-associated death, following Pennsylvania, where a ninth death was reported on Monday, as well as New York and Wisconsin. Pennsylvania's health department mentioned it has now confirmed 1,638 cases across 46 of its counties this year, and noted that only five of those were among individuals vaccinated against the disease.

Recent findings suggest that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, as of a Nov. 19 revision, lists 5,838 confirmed cases of measles this year, well above 2025's total of 2,289. The agency has recognized six of the reported deaths as compared to states' 13, as the federal body mentioned it is looking to develop a standardized definition for deaths due to measles amid disputes over the use and reporting of "measles-associated" deaths.

The United States has lost its measles elimination status, and has now exceeded 5,400 cases and 10 total measles-associated deaths in 2026.

The status determination from the Pan American Health Organization, which is part of the World Health Organization, was made late last week and first reported by the Wall Street Journal before being confirmed by other outlets. (Editor's note: The public health body made its official announcement on Nov. 17).

It has been revealed that the U.S. had notched elimination status, reflecting no continuous spread of the disease for at least 12 months, in 2000. Regaining it similarly requires the country to stop continuous spread for 12 months. PAHO recommends countries that have lost elimination status submit and enact a corrective action plan that includes immunization and surveillance.

Sources indicate that the decision landed shortly after the country hit 5,412 confirmed measles cases, per a Nov. 13 revision from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The federal public health body also lists 591 hospitalizations (11% rate) and six deaths—though it has been hesitant to outright confirm states' reports of measles-associated deaths, of which there have now been 10.

Industry observers note that health groups and public health professionals have pointed to lagging vaccination rates and checked endorsement of routine childhood vaccines from current leadership at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, namely Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., as fueling the country's outbreaks.

The Wisconsin Department of Health Services on Thursday reported its first measles-outbreak associated death since 1990.

The deceased was an infant whose case was among many in the southwestern part of the state, for whom the coroner listed measles as immediate cause of death. As of Nov. 3, the department has reported 431 cases across 13 counties in 2026, the highest number of cases in over 35 years. All but three of those are among individuals who were not vaccinated, and nine have involved hospitalizations.

"Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease," Kirsten Johnson, secretary of the Wisconsin Department of Health Services, said in the announcement. "Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is key for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family.".

As of Oct. 29, the Centers for Disease Control reports 4,852 confirmed cases of measles this year across the country, far outpacing 2025's total of 2,289. Of these, 511 have been hospitalized (versus 244 in 2025) and three deaths have been recognized—though health officials in Pennsylvania alone remarked they have confirmed five measles-associated deaths. The CDC has said its death count may change after it completes work to develop a new standardized case definition for "deaths due to measles.".

The Latest York State Department of Health on Monday afternoon reported its first measles-associated death in 30 years.

The state has counted 210 total cases this year as of Nov. 3. The reported death was a child in the northern Lewis County, according to the department. No information was given about the child's specific illness or the role measles infection may have played in their death.

Sixteen confirmed cases of measles have been reported in Lewis County as of Tuesday, the department said. Many of Latest York's cases are located among upstate counties, and just eight are in New York City, according to the department.

Industry observers note that in a statement, Upcoming York Governor Kathy Hochul—who on Oct. 5 declared a Disaster Emergency in response to rising measles case rates—expressed her sympathies to the child's family and told residents that "vaccination remains our best protection against this dangerous disease.".

"This is New York’s first measles-related death in 30 years, a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses," the statement reads, echoing criticisms of federal health leadership voiced by Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro regarding measles-associated deaths in his own state.

It has been revealed that as of Oct. 29, the Centers for Disease Control reports 4,852 confirmed cases of measles this year across the country, far outpacing 2025's total of 2,289. Of these, 511 have been hospitalized (versus 244 in 2025) and three deaths have been recognized—though health officials in Pennsylvania alone mentioned they have confirmed five measles-associated deaths. The CDC has said its death count may change after it completes work to develop a new standardized case definition for "deaths due to measles.".

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services told Fierce Healthcare that it had deployed epidemiologists and other experts to New York after receiving a formal request for support. The support is presently scheduled to run through Nov. 13, and includes on-the-ground "surveillance, data analysis, strategic planning and other outbreak response support," they noted.

Of the roughly $100 million in additional measles and vaccine-preventable diseases funding the department has provided via the CDC since August, nearly $2.4 million has gone directly to New York State and $2.1 million to New York City, they stated.

"Secretary Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz continue to make clear that the MMR vaccine is the most effective way to prevent measles," they added.

Industry observers note that the U.S. is in the midst of its worst measles outbreak in decades, with more than 4,000 cases reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention as of early October and a sixth measles-associated death disclosed by local Pennsylvania officials on Monday.

Recent findings suggest that the vaccine-preventable disease was declared eliminated in the U.S. back in 2000—meaning that there was no endemic spread of the disease—but has resurfaced in force during recent years as declining childhood vaccination rates have pushed most states below the 95% coverage bar for school-age herd immunity.

The CDC had counted 2,289 cases across the entirety of 2025, which had been the country’s highest total since 1990, and several public health officials have warned for months that number would likely be surpassed based on the scale and frequency of early-year cases.

Measles-associated deaths have also accompanied the higher case counts, though just how many is a subject of dispute. While three deaths were confirmed in all of 2025, this year logged its first in late August with Pennsylvania, which hosts more than a quarter of the total cases, now reporting six measles-associated deaths as of Oct. 13. The CDC, however, lists two deaths alongside a note that its count is subject to change, and has promised more broadly to develop a new, standardized case definition to be used across all reporting states.

That discrepancy is an example of friction between federal health leadership and the broader public health community that experts say has contributed to this year’s outbreaks.

Pennsylvania’s initial death announcements in August were contested by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who accused Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro of withholding sufficient information for the CDC to confirm the deaths and using his press conference announcing them as “gaslighting the public” for political purposes.

During an ensuing social media feud, the governor and the secretary described a heated phone call in which Shapiro (at the time) rejected federal assistance and accused Kennedy of fueling the outbreaks with only lukewarm endorsement of the MMR vaccine and a broader concurrent campaign to scale back other routine childhood vaccinations.

Numerous state public health officials and experts have lobbed similar criticisms of Kennedy, who is affiliated with anti-vaccine groups, and federal health agencies under his purview.

Recent findings suggest that the CDC, for its part, has reportedly infused at least $100 million of extra public health funding to states for immunization programs and surveillance, and leading officials including Kennedy and new CDC Director Erica Schwartz, M.D., have described the MMR vaccine as safe and effective when asked directly. Still, the agency has not launched the type of broader vaccine messaging and awareness campaigns that it would have in years past, critics are quick to note.

Pennsylvania isn’t alone in raising alarms over rising measles cases. Newly introduced York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a State Disaster Emergency in early October, the first such declaration in recent years.

Centralized platform for submitting, managing out-of-network billing disputes launches" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Trump administration has debuted a new online portal for payers, providers and other stakeholders to manage and monitor disputes under the federal Independent Dispute Resolution process.

According to recent reports, the IDR Gateway went online Nov. 13 and was officially unveiled Nov. 20. It replaces the web forms parties previously used to manage disputes, most of which will no longer be available outside of the centralized platform after Jan. 15, 2027, per a government fact sheet.

Payers will eventually be required to register on IDR Gateway so that it is easier for providers to identify the correct party, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services stated earlier this year when finalizing an overhaul of No Surprises Act protocols. That registration feature will be added “in the future on a rolling basis,” CMS said last week, with others like in-portal negotiation similarly rolling out over time “to improve accountability and reduce unnecessary filings,” the agency said last spring.

For now, the IDR Gateway allows parties and their representatives to initiate a dispute, respond to proposed selections of IDR entities and submit a payment offer. Its other tools allow owners to view, search, set up notifications and broadly analyze open disputes for their organization; an IDR Gateway Dashboard, CMS mentioned, offers a color-coded donut chart breaking down an organization’s different types of open disputes by phase, while another tool can generate detailed reports of dispute line items.

Sources indicate that the administration also touted security measures inherent to the new portal. These include a new sign-up process that requires owners to verify their identity with an approved credential service provider, and other protocols like a terms and conditions agreement that notes that unauthorized users could be subject to criminal prosecution.

The baseball-style IDR process enacted under the No Surprises Act, intended to handle out-of-network billing disputes away from the patient’s purview, has become a point of contention amid dispute volumes and payouts well beyond legislators’ expectations.

Arbitrators’ decisions have largely favored providers over payers (85% of decisions went toward providers last year), which alongside court decisions that tweaked CMS’ processes further toward provider preferences, has triggered outright condemnation from payers who have turned to lawsuits, restrictive policies and lobbying in a bit to reform the process. Recent analyses have pegged the IDR process’ impact for employer plans at $8.4 billion in 2025 and total costs associated with the process at $22 billion for that same year.

Lawmakers including the No Surprises Act’s chief authors have said they hope to pass fresh legislation to fix or fully replace the IDR process, with December’s must-pass budget bill now looking like a likely vehicle for such a change.

Breaking: Can a Solar Generator Actually Keep Your Lights On During an Outage—or Is It Just Expensive Hype?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (705 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Winter storm season is fast approaching, with even Thanksgiving being primed for power outages across the country.
  • If you’d like to limit its disruption on your everyday life, generators may be top of mind.
  • As you do your research, you may come across solar generators and wonder how they compare to other options.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Winter storm season is fast approaching, with even Thanksgiving being primed for power outages across the country.

If you’d like to limit its disruption on your everyday life, generators may be top of mind.

As you do your research, you may come across solar generators and wonder how they compare to other options.

“A solar generator uses sunlight as its fuel. It also happens to be clean, quiet, and quick,” explains Ben Zook, founder and owner of Belmont Solar, a solar installation organization in Gordonville, PA.

While a solar generator will likely be more expensive upfront, it could be a smart investment, depending on your location and goals.

By understanding how it works as well as its limitations, you can decide whether it’s the right backup solution for your home.

The name “solar generator” is a bit misleading.

This device is actually a portable battery system you can refill with solar panels and use when you don’t have power.

Recent findings suggest that it includes a built-in inverter that converts DC electricity into AC electricity, which most household appliances use. In addition, it might come with USB ports to charge electronic devices such as cellphones.

So, how does the recharging process work?

“Put simply, solar panels convert sunlight into electricity. When sunlight hits the panels, it produces an electric current,” explains Fox Swim, senior industry researcher at Aurora Solar in Nanaimo, British Columbia.

Keep in mind that a solar generator doesn’t provide unlimited power. It’s limited by your battery’s capacity and how much electricity your panels can produce.

Fortunately, solar generators have evolved over the years and started to incorporate more powerful inverters and larger-capacity batteries.

“Some of the more expensive portable solar generators can now be wired into a home’s main wiring with a transfer switch and provide enough power to run a home's critical loads, like refrigerators, lights, and internet modems for multiple hours or even days,” states Daniel Moyer, a senior trainer with Briggs & Stratton Energy Solutions in Arcata, CA.

Portable gas and propane generators are usually cheaper than portable solar generators.

It has been revealed that "For a high-quality portable gas or propane generator, budget around $700 to $1,000. Comparable solar generators are going to cost you closer to $1,000 to $1,500,” notes Mike Feazel, CEO of Roof Maxx in Westerville, OH.

While portable gas and propane backups could save you some cash, they do come with drawbacks that are notable to consider.

“These options are noisy, produce exhaust that must be vented properly, and demand regular maintenance. In addition, they require you to buy and safely store fuel,” Swim says.

Solar generations generally cost more to buy and install, but there are a few reasons for this.

“The panels are quieter as they have no moving parts, require less frequent maintenance, and don’t rely on fuel,” Fox adds.

One of the major downsides of solar generators, however, is that they may produce significantly less electricity during winter, depending on where you live.

Fox’s simulations show just how much production can vary.

In Boise, ID, a 1-kilowatt solar generator produces about 176 kilowatt-hours in a typical June compared to just 66 in December.

In Huntington Beach, CA, the same setup generates 156 kilowatt-hours in June and 127 in December.

Industry observers note that so, how do you know whether solar backup is a smart resilience investment or overkill for your needs? It comes down to your unique situation and goals.

To make the most informed decision, ask yourself what you’d need to power if the electricity goes out and how often that would probably happen.

“If you only lose power a couple of times a year and mainly want the fridge, internet, and some lights on, a solar generator makes a lot of sense,” explains Feazel.

However, if your goal is to power your entire home and you live somewhere with frequent, prolonged outages, a solar generator may not be powerful enough. You might be better off with a whole-home generator.

“If you’re unsure, consult a reputable solar installer about your budget and your expectations for backup time and what you need powered during an outage. They can point you in the right direction,” adds Moyer.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that in a letter to tech giant employees, Ramaswami (pictured) noted he’s going to continue in the role for the time being while he works with Nutanix’s board of directors to identify a successor and assist with the transition.
  • Ramaswami, who is 60 years old, did not give any reason for his coming departure, but the letter seems to indicate that he’s not ready to retire just yet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:54 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Rajiv Ramaswami is stepping down from his role as chief executive of Nutanix Inc., six years after he joined the hyperconverged cloud infrastructure company from its rival VMware Inc.

Recent findings suggest that in a letter to tech giant employees, Ramaswami (pictured) noted he’s going to continue in the role for the time being while he works with Nutanix’s board of directors to identify a successor and assist with the transition. “After that, I will continue to serve as a senior advisor to the company for a period of time,” he said in the letter.

Ramaswami, who is 60 years old, did not give any reason for his coming departure, but the letter seems to indicate that he’s not ready to retire just yet.

According to recent reports, “Our next CEO will inherit a strong platform, a loyal customer base and, most importantly, an exceptional team,” Ramaswami wrote. “Until then, my focus remains on leading this manufacturer and nothing about our day-to-day priorities changes. I am committed to helping our next leader succeed, and my ask of you, as always, is to continue to focus on executing as we go through this leadership transition.”.

Ramaswami added that Nutanix has hired an executive search firm to lead the hunt for his successor. The news came as the tech giant delivered its first-quarter earnings report, posting modest year-over-year gains in profit and revenue.

The firm reported adjusted earnings of 73 cents per share, beating Wall Street’s target of 61 cents per share by a strong margin. Revenue for the period came to $772.4 million, up 15% from a year earlier and above the Street’s forecast of $762.7 million.

Industry observers note that nutanix’s outlook for the current quarter is strong, with the manufacturer guiding for sales of between $820 million and $830 million, compared with the Street’s consensus estimate of $820.4 million. However, the full-year picture is a little less rosy, with Nutanix guiding for annual sales of $3.18 billion to $3.23 billion. The midpoint of that range trails the Street’s forecast of $3.22 billion in fiscal 2027 revenue.

Industry observers note that investors did not take the news very well. The cautious full-year guidance compared with the uncertainty over leadership prompted many to sell, and Nutanix’s stock was down 8% after-hours, having already fallen more than 5% during the regular trading session, on a down day for many tech stocks.

Virginia Gambale, of the board at Nutanix, hailed the “tremendous impact” Ramaswami had on the company during his six-year tenure. “Rajiv led the company’s transformation to subscription software, built a loyal and expanding global enterprise base and established a technology portfolio that we believe positions us well for the AI era,” she said. “We’re focused on selecting an exceptional leader who can build on that foundation.”.

Sources indicate that in a conference call with analysts, Ramaswami said he believes the organization is embarking on the third major chapter in its history. The first chapter, before his arrival, saw the company establish itself as the leader of the hyperconverged infrastructure industry. Chapter two began when he took over, and saw Nutanix expand from those roots to become a platform company, he said.

“[We have] transformed the tech giant to be profitable while growing and expanding the product portfolio quite significantly, from HCI to a platform that works across clouds, supports external storage and has cloud-native capabilities and now moving into the future with AI capabilities,” Ramaswami stated. “Chapter two is well-established at this point and there’s a lot of opportunity in terms of driving growth. I feel like we are in a very good place.”.

Sources indicate that according to Ramaswami, Nutanix now stands at an inflection point as it looks to cash in on the newly introduced era of artificial intelligence. “I’ve been talking to the board for a bit about this, as well as in terms of our strategic direction and the timing for succession, and so we came to the conclusion together that this is perhaps the right time,” he told analysts. “[We wanted] to announce it ahead of time as we look for the appropriate next leader.”.

In a recent development, ramaswami’s departure from the company should at least be a lot smoother than his arrival. Nutanix unveiled it had appointed Ramaswami as its CEO in late 2020, just two days after he quit his role as chief operating officer of its biggest rival, VMware.

VMware was indignant about the manner of his departure, and responded with a lawsuit that accused Ramaswami of breaching his legal and contractual duties to the company by “secretly meeting” with Nutanix’s board to discuss taking over, while continuing to play a leading role in shaping its product and business strategy. The lawsuit was ultimately settled out of court about a year later.

In April, Ramaswami appeared on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s mobile livestreaming studio, where he talked about how Nutanix is shifting away from HCI to focus on more of a “disaggregated infrastructure” strategy to support demand for autonomous AI agents:.

Cannabis addiction linked to 57% higher odds of suicidal thoughts

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (944 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As marijuana becomes more widely available and accepted, researchers are uncovering important questions about its effects on mental health.
  • Published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, the research found that adults with cannabis use disorder had 57% higher odds of reporting suicidal thoughts compared with those without the condition.
  • According to recent reports, the findings come from an analysis of more than 415,000 American adults who participated in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As marijuana becomes more widely available and accepted, researchers are uncovering important questions about its effects on mental health. A major fresh study suggests that people who struggle to control their cannabis use face a substantially greater likelihood of experiencing suicidal thoughts.

Published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, the research found that adults with cannabis use disorder had 57% higher odds of reporting suicidal thoughts compared with those without the condition. Despite major shifts in marijuana laws and public attitudes, this troubling association remained remarkably consistent over a decade.

According to recent reports, the findings come from an analysis of more than 415,000 American adults who participated in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health. Researchers examined data collected between 2014 and 2023, a period when cannabis became increasingly accessible across the United States.

Sources indicate that "What surprised me most was not that cannabis use disorder was associated with suicidal thoughts, but that this association did not appear to strengthen over time," said lead author Tosin Philip Oyetunji, MPH, a doctoral student in public health at the University of California, Merced. "[Yet,] it remains an key mental health concern that deserves attention.".

Cannabis and Suicidal Thoughts Show a Persistent Link.

Sources indicate that the connection between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thinking was observed across different age groups, sexes, and racial and ethnic backgrounds. However, women and younger adults revealed particularly elevated risks.

Importantly, the association remained even after researchers accounted for depression, psychological distress, and other factors that could influence mental health outcomes.

The consistency of the results was especially notable given how dramatically the cannabis landscape has changed. Recreational marijuana is now legal in half of U.S. states, and cannabis products have become increasingly potent. These developments have raised concerns among public health experts about whether broader access might contribute to worsening mental health.

Yet the study offers some reassurance on that particular question. Sidra Goldman-Mellor, PhD, a professor of public health at UC Merced and the study's senior author, noted that the association between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thoughts did not become stronger during the 10 years examined.

Industry observers note that "Suicidal ideation does not seem to have increased among people with cannabis use disorder, despite all this legal and social change," explained Goldman-Mellor. Yet, "people with cannabis use disorder are still at a very substantially increased likelihood of experiencing serious suicidal thoughts, and that's not something that is widely understood.".

Why Cannabis Use Disorder Matters.

The researchers stress that these findings should not be interpreted as evidence that everyone who uses marijuana faces the same elevated risk.

Industry observers note that the study focused specifically on cannabis use disorder, a condition in which people have difficulty controlling their marijuana consumption even when it causes problems in their lives. Someone with the disorder may continue using cannabis despite harmful consequences or repeated attempts to cut back.

This distinction is vital because problematic cannabis use differs from occasional or otherwise nonproblematic consumption.

Sources indicate that the findings also do not establish that cannabis use disorder directly causes suicidal thoughts. Because the research identified an association rather than a cause-and-effect relationship, it cannot determine whether problematic cannabis use contributes to suicidal thinking, whether underlying mental health difficulties contribute to both conditions, or whether other factors help explain the connection.

Nevertheless, the results point to a significant mental health concern that deserves greater recognition, particularly among people seeking help for problematic cannabis use.

Researchers Urge Greater Mental Health Screening.

One practical implication is that health care professionals should look beyond cannabis consumption itself when evaluating patients with cannabis use disorder.

Rather than focusing exclusively on depression or substance use symptoms, clinicians may benefit from asking patients directly about suicidal thoughts as part of a broader mental health assessment. This could help identify people who need additional care but whose struggles might otherwise remain unnoticed.

It has been revealed that "Someone seeking help for cannabis use disorder may also be experiencing suicidal thoughts that are not immediately apparent," said Oyetunji. "The goal is not to assume that everyone with cannabis use disorder is suicidal but to identify those who may need additional assessment, treatment, or support.".

The study arrives at a time when marijuana is increasingly viewed as a relatively low-risk substance. Public perceptions have shifted considerably, and negative attitudes toward cannabis have declined alongside expanding legalization and social acceptance.

However, these changes have not eliminated the mental health challenges associated with cannabis use disorder. Even though the strength of the association with suicidal thoughts did not increase over the study period, the elevated odds remained substantial.

The researchers suggest that health care providers, policymakers, and community organizations can play an crucial role by improving awareness, identifying vulnerable individuals, and making appropriate mental health support more accessible.

As attitudes toward marijuana continue to evolve, the findings serve as a reminder that the needs of people experiencing problematic cannabis use should remain a public health priority.

Said Oyetunji, "As cannabis becomes more accessible and socially accepted, we should ensure that the people struggling with its use are not overlooked.".

Why Is Crypto Down Today? Cryptocurrency markets woke up red on Tuesday, November 24, 2026. Bitcoin slipped below the psychologically important $60,000 level, trading near $59,800–$60,500 after briefly touching levels above $64,000 the day before.

Ethereum, Solana, and most major altcoins followed lower, with the total crypto market capitalization contracting roughly 1–2% over 24 hours amid elevated liquidations and persistent selling pressure. The question on every trader’s mind is straightforward: why is crypto down today?

It has been revealed that crypto entered the week already wounded. Bitcoin had plunged to a multi-year low near $55,000 over the prior weekend, wiping out leveraged positions and leaving the market in extreme fear territory.

Recent findings suggest that monday brought a sharp relief rally. Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO sent the chipmaker’s shares soaring more than 30% and lifted the Nasdaq by around 7%. Risk assets broadly benefited, and Bitcoin briefly joined the party, climbing toward $64,000.

That bounce proved short-lived. By Tuesday morning, the gains had been fully erased. Bitcoin lagged the equity rebound significantly; Nvidia recovered most of its recent losses, while crypto reclaimed only a fraction of its slide. The divergence highlighted that crypto’s problems run deeper than a single day’s equity news.

According to recent reports, several concrete developments converged to pressure prices. First, the Nvidia-driven rally simply faded. Stock futures turned lower on Tuesday as the initial euphoria cooled.

Industry observers note that nasdaq-100 futures dropped around 1%, and related AI and crypto-adjacent equities gave back part of Monday’s gains. Crypto, which had been riding the coattails of the tech surge, sold off in sympathy but more sharply.

In a recent development, second, institutional flows remained deeply negative. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded approximately $570M in net outflows on Monday, the fifth consecutive session of withdrawals.

BlackRock’s IBIT alone accounted for more than $500M of that figure. November’s cumulative outflows reached roughly $4.71Bn, setting a monthly record and removing a major source of structural demand that had previously supported prices.

Third, derivatives markets amplified the move. More than $800M in crypto futures positions were liquidated over the 24-hour period, more than triple the prior day’s total. Forced selling from both long and short positions created a self-reinforcing cascade as prices fell.

It has been revealed that broader macro factors also weighed on sentiment. Markets continue to price in a potential Federal Reserve rate hike in December, with key inflation data (PCE) due shortly.

Higher rates typically pressure non-yielding assets such as Bitcoin. Additional reports of possible newly introduced U.S. tariff measures added another layer of risk-off caution. Lingering effects from the large Binance-related hack earlier in the period further eroded confidence in the sector.

Crypto’s decline today is not the result of a single dramatic headline. Instead, it reflects a short-term relief rally that failed to overcome persistent structural headwinds.

In a recent development, the Nvidia news provided temporary momentum, but without positive ETF flows or a meaningful shift in monetary expectations, that momentum evaporated quickly. Leveraged traders were caught offside, and the resulting liquidations accelerated the drop.

Sentiment remains extremely cautious. The Fear & Greed Index sits deep in extreme fear, at around 10/100, and Bitcoin has still only recovered a modest portion of its November losses.

While some long-term holders and selective buyers may view current levels as attractive, the immediate market is dominated by risk reduction and profit-taking after the failed bounce.

Crypto is down today primarily because Monday’s Nvidia-fueled rally proved unsustainable. Heavy, record-setting Bitcoin ETF outflows continued to drain demand, while a surge in futures liquidations forced additional selling.

It has been revealed that macro uncertainty around interest rates and risk assets provided no supporting backdrop. In short, the market tested a bounce, found insufficient real buying interest, and retreated—leaving Bitcoin back below $60,000 and the broader crypto complex lower.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Derek Hough is opening up about his upbringing, sharing painful details from his childhood in his new Hulu documentary, “The Symphony of Dance.”.

In the film, the “Dancing with the Stars" judge returns to his childhood home in Utah, and details the challenging environment he was raised in.

Industry observers note that “The neighborhood that we grew up in, we definitely just had some neighbors that weren’t great,” Derek, 41, explained. “They pretty much terrorized my family in a lot of ways.”.

In a recent development, “They hung me up in a tree by my ankles. They put a gun to my head, spat on me, hogtied me up in a field and left me there,” he continued. “One of my neighbors was, for lack of a better word, really inappropriate with me, physically.”.

Eventually, Derek’s parents separated, and the family moved across town to an apartment building where his mother and father lived in units across the hall from one another.

It has been revealed that “I remember moving away from there and feeling relieved,” he mentioned. However, the move didn’t solve all of his problems, and he continued to struggle in the wake of his parents’ divorce.

Sources indicate that “I just didn’t understand where I was going. I didn’t understand what I was doing,” he said. “I was just kind of left to my own devices as a 12-year-old. I would skip school. I would skip dance, just floating around with no direction.”.

Although he had initially pushed back when his parents wanted to enroll him in dance classes, Derek explained that the artform eventually became his “safe haven”—and his ticket to a upcoming life in London.

When renowned dancers Corky and Shirley Ballas—who “Dancing with the Stars” fans will recognize as the parents of pro Mark Ballas—visited Derek’s dance studio, they saw that he had something special.

“We saw the gift, we saw the talent, and we saw the struggle that his family was having at the time,” Shirley recalled in her documentary interview. “But more than that, he indicated his dedication to the art. You could see it from a very, very young age.”.

Shirley explained that this potential is what motivated the Ballas family to take Derek under their wings.

“He needed an opportunity. He needed a place to grow. And I remember him walking in, after the end of one of the classes, and saying to me, ‘Can I come and live with you?’” Shirley said. “We spoke to [his father] Bruce, he thought that was a good idea for Derek to live with us in London for a short space of time.”.

Recent findings suggest that the arrangement—in which Derek was enrolled in the Italia Conti Performing Arts Academy with Mark—was initially planned to last just six months. But Derek’s father said that by Christmas of that year, the Ballas family suggested bringing sister Julianne Hough over, too.

At the time, Julianne was 10 and Derek was 12.

Industry observers note that “I felt like moving away was great because I was getting away from something,” Derek explained. “I was leaving like, this wounded boy, and I was going to go become this success. I was gonna work hard and achieve things and overcome things.”.

The stay kept getting extended as Derek became more dedicated to ballroom dancing.

“I every year, sort of begged them to come home, and they begged to stay,” Bruce said of his children’s move to London.

Derek and Julianne felt very at home overseas, however.

It has been revealed that “It was almost like this ritual. Every summer we would go home, and my dad was like, ‘Yo, it’s time to come home, You guys. I wanna raise you. You’re my kids. I want you to be here,” Derek said. “And it was honestly this fight where I was like, ‘We’re on this path, and I’m gonna win this championship if I keep going here and going in this direction.”.

Derek would ultimately stay in London—and win a handful of titles—until 2007, when he returned to the United States full time and joined the cast of “Dancing with the Stars.”.

  • Why Parkinson's Treatment Often Requires Brain Implants.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An international research team has developed a fresh technique that uses magnetic fields and tiny particles to stimulate regions deep inside the brain, potentially opening the door to a less invasive treatment for Parkinson's disease. In experiments involving mice with Parkinson's-like symptoms, the approach significantly improved movement problems without requiring permanently implanted electrodes.

The technique involves injecting specially designed magnetic nanoplatelets into a targeted area of the brain. When exposed to an external magnetic field, these particles generate tiny forces that activate nearby nerve cells. Unlike conventional brain stimulation treatments, which rely on surgically implanted electrodes, the fresh approach uses magnetic forces to influence brain activity. The findings, published in Advanced Science, come from researchers at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU), RWTH Aachen, and the Universities of Maastricht (the Netherlands) and Leuven (Belgium).

Why Parkinson's Treatment Often Requires Brain Implants.

It has been revealed that parkinson's disease develops as brain cells responsible for producing dopamine gradually break down. Dopamine is a chemical messenger that plays a vital role in controlling movement. As its levels decline, communication within the brain's movement circuits becomes disrupted, contributing to tremors and other motor difficulties.

Recent findings suggest that for some patients, deep brain stimulation can help control these symptoms. This treatment uses a device known as a brain pacemaker, which is implanted beneath the collarbone and connected to electrodes placed deep inside the brain. The electrodes deliver electrical stimulation to a region called the subthalamic nucleus (STN for short), helping to modify abnormal activity in the brain circuits responsible for movement.

Although this treatment can provide substantial relief, it requires a complex surgical procedure and does not work for everyone.

"The procedure is relatively complex, however, and not always successful," explains Prof. Dr. Danijela Gregurec from the Department of Chemistry and Pharmacy at FAU. "This puts many Parkinson's patients off, and not all patients are suitable candidates for one of these pacemakers.".

The researchers believe magnetic stimulation could eventually provide another option, allowing doctors to influence the same deep brain structures without leaving electrodes permanently implanted.

How Tiny Magnetic Particles Stimulate Brain Cells.

The upcoming technology takes advantage of the ability of certain nerve cells to detect physical pressure and mechanical forces.

"We use magnetic nanoparticles that we implant in the brain," Gregurec explains. "They have a special shape and a magnetic structure. They were developed in order to transform magnetic fields into tiny mechanical forces.".

Rather than sending electrical pulses directly into the brain, the technique uses these particles to produce extremely small physical movements when a magnetic field is applied.

"The traditional method establishes an electrical connection to the brain," she notes. "In contrast, we use the neurons' natural mechanosensors to influence regions deep within the brain.".

Industry observers note that the process works by gently changing the shape of nearby nerve cell membranes. Imagine pressing a finger against an inflated balloon and creating a small indentation in its surface. The magnetic particles produce a similar effect on a microscopic scale.

This slight deformation opens specialized channels in the cell membrane that respond to mechanical pressure. Once opened, these channels allow electrically charged particles called ions to enter the nerve cells, changing their electrical activity and providing a way to stimulate the targeted brain circuits.

Magnetic Brain Stimulation Improves Movement in Mice.

It has been revealed that to investigate whether the technology could relieve Parkinson's symptoms, the international research team conducted experiments using mice with damage to the same types of dopamine-producing nerve cells affected by the disease in humans. This damage caused movement difficulties resembling those seen in Parkinson's patients.

In a recent development, "Together with our partners from Maastricht, we injected magnetic nanoparticles developed here at FAU into the animals' subthalamic nucleus," Gregurec explains. "That is the very region in the brain that is also an notable target for conventional deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease.".

The researchers used precise stereotactic injection techniques to deliver the particles to the intended location. These methods rely on carefully calculated three-dimensional coordinates to guide instruments into specific brain structures. Accurate placement was particularly vital because the treatment needed to affect the correct neural circuits involved in movement.

Sources indicate that after the particles were positioned, the researchers applied an external magnetic field. The results were encouraging: the mice showed significant improvements in their movement deficits.

"The effect is roughly equivalent to what we would have expected after implanting a brain pacemaker," states Gregurec.

The findings suggest that magnetic nanoparticles could provide a different way to achieve some of the benefits of conventional deep brain stimulation, without the need for permanently implanted electrodes.

Could Future Parkinson's Treatments Use Magnetic Headbands?

Another encouraging finding involved how the brain responded to the implanted particles over time. The magnetic nanoparticles remained in place throughout an observation period lasting several months, and the researchers found no signs of inflammation. This suggests that the particles were well tolerated during the experiments.

However, delivering the particles still required an injection directly into the brain. Gregurec and her colleagues are now investigating ways to make the procedure even less invasive.

One possibility is to develop particles that could be injected into the bloodstream and then travel into the brain by crossing the blood-brain barrier. This protective boundary normally prevents many substances circulating in the blood from entering brain tissue. Finding a way to deliver the particles across it could eliminate the need for direct brain injections.

The researchers are also exploring compact wearable devices capable of generating the magnetic fields needed for stimulation. One possibility is a headband that patients could put on themselves, potentially making treatment more convenient and adjustable.

These ideas remain at an early stage, and the researchers expect that several more years of development will be needed before the technology could be considered for clinical use.

According to recent reports, "Nevertheless, we are convinced that the fresh method has enormous potential," Gregurec states. "It is not only considerably simpler and cheaper than a conventional brain pacemaker, it is probably also more flexible. Adjusting the parameters of the magnetic field would allow us to control the nanoparticles more accurately.".

Beyond its potential medical applications, the technology could also become a valuable scientific tool. By allowing researchers to stimulate nerve cells through carefully controlled mechanical forces, it offers a newly introduced way to explore how physical changes at the cellular level influence brain activity.

Although the treatment has so far been demonstrated only in animals, its ability to improve movement without permanently implanted electrodes represents a promising step toward new approaches to Parkinson's disease and brain stimulation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Academic hospital heads petition Congress for 2-year delay to CMS' 340B cuts" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Dozens of academic health system and teaching hospital chief executives are turning to Congress in a bid to blunt a controversial subsidy cut coming to Medicare Part B in the fresh year.

Earlier this month, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services locked in intends to reduce reimbursements for outpatient drugs dispensed by participants in the 340B Drug Pricing Program during the 2027 calendar year.

Specifically, the agency stated it will move from the current rate of average sales price (ASP) plus 6% down to ASP minus 28%, with a corresponding 7.5% increase in non-drug outpatient payments to maintain budget neutrality. CMS said the change will reduce Original Medicare drug payments by an estimated $4.35 billion and drug payments from beneficiaries by $1.1 billion during the policy’s first year.

Hospital groups—particularly those that chiefly represent nonprofit or safety-net hospitals—have denounced the plan’s disproportionate effect on hospitals participating in the decades-old subsidy program, as well as a gift to for-profit hospitals that do not participate but will benefit from the budget-neutral offset.

With their formal opposition to the policy’s proposal set aside by CMS, 95 executives whose organizations are members of the Association of American Medical Colleges have now penned a letter to leaders of the House and the Senate pleading for a two-year delay to the rate cut’s implementation.

“This policy will exacerbate already negative Medicare margins at a time when teaching hospitals are already grappling with rising financial challenges resulting from inflation, workforce shortages, manufacturer-driven restrictions on the 340B program and an expected rise in uncompensated care costs,” they wrote.

It has been revealed that the executives acknowledged that the final policy’s rate of ASP minus 28% is “slightly smaller” than CMS’ initial proposal of ASP minus 33.4%, but said the change was still a threat to the country’s healthcare safety net. They noted the cuts represent a nearly $5.5 billion reduction that would be disproportionately shouldered by AAMC-member teaching hospitals—who comprise 17% of all impacted hospitals—but will see almost $3 billion of that total.

Sources indicate that those funds are necessary to finance critical care services at academic hospitals including trauma care, inpatient behavioral care, transplant surgery and labor and delivery, the signatories warned lawmakers. They also noted that their institutions are major referral hubs that accept “the most complex transfer cases from lower acuity settings, such as rural and community hospitals,” in a way that for-profit hospitals and others who will benefit from the final rule do not.

“While we understand that Congress has an interest in improving the 340B program, and are broadly supportive of meaningful transparency and accountability for covered entities, we also strongly believe that cutting Medicare payment to 340B hospitals is not the appropriate policy mechanism to achieve these goals,” they wrote. “Therefore, we respectfully request that you support a two-year delay in the [Outpatient Prospective Payment System] rule’s payment cuts for 340B-acquired drugs.”.

Among the letter’s 95 signatories were the heads of Cedars-Sinai, Stanford Health Care, Yale New Haven Health, Tampa General Hospital, Rush University System for Health, Mass General Brigham, Nebraska Medicine, RWJBarnabas Health, NewYork-Presbyterian, UNC Health and School of Medicine, OHSU, Jefferson Health, Penn Medicine, Vanderbilt Health and Froedtert ThedaCare.

The academic health systems and hospitals’ turn to lawmakers comes after their rebukes of CMS’ 340B policy have fallen on deaf ears. The agency and broader Trump administration have often sided with critics of the subsidy program on related initiatives like a pilot rebate program, citing 340B’s rapid growth and contribution to increased healthcare spending. A Health and Human Services Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation policy brief defending the rate cut made those views crystal clear with claims that the program has incentivized provider consolidation while doing little to serve patients’ needs.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, Congress, spurred by public pressure to reduce healthcare costs, has proposed its own legislative fixes to 340B. Though each bill aims to preserve the program and subsidize safety-net care, some are more friendly to the hospital industry than others.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jessica Alba’s divorce from Cash Warren is back in the headlines after a fresh court order awarded Warren $577,481 from Alba’s retirement benefits.

The ruling comes after the former couple sold their longtime Beverly Hills–area home and Alba later purchased another property in the area.

In a recent development, the retirement award comes from Alba’s account in the HonorBar Inc. Profit Sharing Initiative, according to court documents reported by TMZ.

Sources indicate that any money left in the account after Warren receives his share is to go to Alba. The documents also allow Warren to take the award as a lump sum or move it into an individual retirement account or another retirement proposal.

The court order also addresses account records: If Warren requests statements in writing within the next year, Alba must provide them within 10 days.

According to the outlet, transferring the money into a retirement account could avoid a 20% tax withholding.

The ruling is the latest financial development following the couple’s divorce, which was finalized in February 2026.

It was previously reported that Alba was ordered to pay Warren $3 million to balance the division of their assets.

Their settlement also divided interests in several companies, shares in The Honest Manufacturer, and residuals from projects made during their marriage.

Meanwhile, Alba and Warren have already put their real estate ties behind them.

According to recent reports, their former Beverly Hills–area home was sold in 2025. Alba and Warren purchased the seven-bedroom estate for $9.9 million in 2017, then put it on the market in April 2025 for $18.99 million. It was sold for $18.2 million, with the closing recorded on June 27, 2025.

The property sat on about 1.86 acres and included 8.5 bathrooms, a guesthouse, a home theater, and extensive grounds.

Alba and Warren undertook an 18-month renovation after buying it, with Alba involved in decisions about the home’s design.

The estate had been a family residence for years, and Alba spoke about the family’s plans for the house during a 2019 Architectural Digest tour.

After the sale, Alba picked up a splashy Beverly Hills estate in September 2025 for $4.75 million.

The roughly 5,000-square-foot property boasts four bedrooms, five bathrooms, tiled roofing, and modern amenities.

The two transactions mark a change in Alba’s recent housing history: the end of her and Warren’s ownership of a sprawling family estate, followed by her purchase of another Beverly Hills property.

Alba and Warren announced their separation in December 2024 after 16 years of marriage.

Alba filed for divorce citing irreconcilable differences, and the sale of their longtime home followed the announcement.

The latest retirement-benefit order concerns a separate part of their financial settlement, while the Beverly Hills transactions provide a look at the real estate changes that accompanied their split.

Latest Update: Inside Elizabeth Holmes’ Secret Oceanfront Rental Seen in ‘You Can See Everything’ Documentary a Month Before She’s Sent to Prison

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” takes place in the Theranos founder’s former Del Mar, CA, rental—and the property’s location in an exclusive, gated community could be just part of the reason the film’s unexpected release was such a smash.

The project—which is now available to stream on demand and was directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim—was kept secret for the four years it was in production, leaving viewers in awe after the documentary’s surprise Sept. 6 premiere at Telluride Film Festival.

Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, invited the film crew—which Oppenheim told Variety was intentionally kept intimate to keep the project a secret—to reside in the guesthouse of the home for the 34 days before she reported to Federal Prison Camp in Bryan, TX, on May 30, 2023.

“Keeping it under wraps was very important because we never wanted to get in front of what we were capturing,” the director shared.

The crew would typically shoot for 16-hour days, with Fielder telling Variety that cameras were strategically positioned to “cover the whole house” so nothing would be missed.

According to recent reports, the four-bedroom, four-bathroom beachfront property is located in an ultraprivate community less than a half-hour from San Diego. Called Sandy Lane, it features just about a dozen residences.

“This is basically a hidden community. It’s a guard-gated community, which is so rare on a beach, which is why you have a lot of high-profile individuals up and down this strip,” celebrity real estate agent Josh Altman explained in a home tour of another property on the community’s sole street.

Given the home's private location—and considering California’s anti-paparazzi legislation protecting private property from capture—it’s plain to see why Holmes and Evans opted to rent the 2,200-square-foot dwelling in the time leading up to her imprisonment.

According to recent reports, the New York Times also previously reported that the couple and their two children moved to the area to be nearer to Evans’ family. His parents, William L. Evans and Susan Evans, are the hotel magnates behind Evans Hotels, a San Diego–based hospitality organization.

Although the property is presently off-market, a previous listing indicates the single-story home was built in 1948 and includes direct access to the private beach.

As seen in the film, the abode features tall ceilings with exposed-beams and sizable windows connecting the home to the serene surrounding landscape. Midcentury modern design is present throughout the home, which is paneled in honey-hued wood.

Sources indicate that while Realtor.com® estimates the property’s current market value to be about $5.8 million, it’s unclear just how much Holmes and Evans shelled out to reside there temporarily. The most recent publicly listed rent was $5,650 a month in 2015, which is a decrease from the $5,950 rent it was listed for in 2012.

The Sandy Lane spot is not the only prominent rental property Holmes has retreated to since her legal troubles began. During her trial from Aug. 31, 2021, to Jan. 3, 2022, she resided in one of the seven homes of San Francisco’s notable Green Gables.

The sprawling 74-acre property was owned by the Fleishhacker family for over a century before it was sold for a record-breaking $85 million in 2025.

Before Theranos came crumbling down, Holmes and her former business and romantic partner, Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani, purchased a $9 million French provincial manor in Atherton, a wealthy enclave of Silicon Valley.

Privacy was likely a factor in that decision, as well, as the five-bedroom, 5.5-bathroom mansion was set behind a gated entrance and tall trees.

The home was considerably more lavish than the beach bungalow that serves as the backdrop for “You Can See Everything,” with a 6,800-square-foot main home accompanied by gardens, a pool, and a pavilion on a 1.16-acre lot.

Along with the couple’s young children, Evans has since relocated from California to Texas, so the family can visit Holmes in prison, where she is serving an 11-year sentence for three counts of wire fraud and one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud.

The sentence was reduced to nine years for good behavior, and Holmes has since been approved for placement in a community correction center, ABC News reported, citing an revision from the Department of Justice's Victim Notification System.

Holmes is scheduled to be placed in the Austin Transitional Center in De Valle, TX, in August 2027.
